claims.text: Greg Short asserts that building for volume — creating a product that solves problems for a massive number of people with ordinary spending habits — is one of the greatest business opportunities available today, rather than targeting small premium niches. His reasoning is that products used by ordinary people at ordinary price points generate organic word-of-mouth referrals at scale, compounding reach in ways that niche high-ticket products cannot.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: Applies to founder thinking about long-term career legacy, not necessarily early-stage product selection
claims.mechanism: Ordinary-priced products that solve widespread problems get used daily and referred naturally; word-of-mouth compounds at scale when the addressable audience is measured in millions or billions rather than thousands.
bounded_by: Greg Short acknowledges you can start niche early-stage; the claim applies to career-level vision, not necessarily the first product

claims.text: Greg Short observes that the majority of outrageously successful entrepreneurs he knows personally have built businesses selling products or solving problems for ordinary people with ordinary spending habits, not for wealthy or premium buyer segments.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: Based on Greg Short's personal network and circle; not a population-representative sample
bounded_by: Greg Short explicitly qualifies this as possibly a selection artifact of his own network: 'maybe they just happen to be in my network and my circle'

claims.text: Greg Short argues that thinking big about your career vision does not mean building expensive products; the scale of the problem solved and the size of the addressable market matter more than the price point of the offer. He cites energy drinks as an example of a product with over a billion potential buyers globally.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: Applies to founders designing their long-term business career, not single-product decisions

numbers.axis: potential buyer base for a single product category

examples.text: Greg Short uses energy drinks as a concrete illustration of a mass-market product: over a billion people globally drink energy drinks, making the category an example of the scale achievable when you build for ordinary people with ordinary spending habits rather than premium niches.

practices.text: When designing your long-term career vision, think about building a product that solves a problem for the largest possible number of people — not just the most expensive one you can imagine.
You can start niche in the early stage, but hold a larger vision for your eventual market: products that ordinary people actually use and refer to friends compound growth at scale.
